title: Pinning and the POH
sub: fixed, GCHandle, Memory.Pin and the pinned object heap
cards/0/title: Why stop the collector from moving an object
cards/0/body:
During compaction the collector slides surviving objects and rewrites every reference to them. Managed code never notices: references are updated and everything works.

But native code — an OS function, a C library, a network card driver — holds a raw address. The collector cannot see it and will not update it. If the object has moved, native code writes its data over someone else’s object.

So before handing an address out, you pin the object: you tell the collector "do not move this one". A pinned object stays put until the pin is released.
cards/0/deep: The P/Invoke marshaller pins blittable arrays and strings by itself for the duration of a synchronous call — you write nothing extra. The trouble starts when native code remembers the address for longer than one call: asynchronous I/O, callbacks, driver ring buffers. Then the lifetime of the pin is your job.
cards/1/title: fixed: a pin for the length of a block
cards/1/body:
The cheapest way is the fixed statement in unsafe code. It gives you a pointer to the data and pins the object until the end of the block.

The mechanism: the compiler puts the reference into a local variable marked pinned. There is no runtime call at all. Only if a collection happens during the block does the collector, walking the stack, see the mark and leave the object in place.

The cost is close to zero when no collection happened. The limitation: the pointer is valid only inside the block; after the } the object may move again.
cards/1/deep:
In IL this is a local like uint8& pinned: a managed pointer to the first element. The JIT records in the method’s GC info that the slot is pinned, and the collector learns it while walking frames. For string, Span<T> and your own types, fixed works through the GetPinnableReference() pattern (C# 7.3).

If the array is empty or null, fixed gives a null pointer rather than an exception.
cards/2/q: The method keeps the pointer it got from fixed. Which line writes to where the array may no longer be?
cards/2/explain: Copying the pointer inside the block is allowed, but after leaving fixed there is no pin. A compacting collection may move data, and the write through saved corrupts someone else’s memory. The compiler does not catch it: to the compiler a pointer is just a number.
cards/3/title: GCHandle: a pin without a scope
cards/3/body:
When you need the address for longer than one method, use GCHandle.Alloc(obj, GCHandleType.Pinned). The runtime creates an entry in the handle table: the collector walks it as roots and does not move pinned objects.

  • AddrOfPinnedObject() returns the address of the data;
  • the pin holds until you call Free(). Forget it and the object is pinned forever and never collected;
  • you can only pin an object without references inside: an array of primitives, a string, a class made of numbers. Otherwise — ArgumentException.
cards/3/deep:
The rule comes from marshalling: only blittable data, which looks the same in the native world, is handed out. References inside an object are useless to native code, and writing to them behind the write barrier’s back would break the collector’s bookkeeping. So the runtime checks the type when pinning.

.NET 10 added typed wrappers GCHandle<T>, PinnedGCHandle<T> and WeakGCHandle<T> with Dispose instead of Free — handy to keep in a using.
cards/4/options/1: Pins the list and its inner array
cards/4/explain: List<int> holds a reference to its _items array, and objects with references cannot be pinned. You can pin the int[] itself — but the list will replace it with a new one when it grows.
cards/4/wrong/1: Pinning does not follow references: each object is pinned on its own.
cards/4/wrong/3: The signature takes object; the compiler does not check whether it can be pinned — the runtime does.
cards/5/body:
Span<T> lives only on the stack and cannot cross an await. In async code a buffer travels as Memory<T>, and you get its address through Pin().

Pin() returns a MemoryHandle with a Pointer field. Until the handle is released with Dispose(), the data does not move. Under the hood, for an ordinary array it is the same GCHandle; for native memory there is nothing to pin, and Pin is almost free.
cards/5/deep: If the array already lives in the POH, an extra GCHandle is not needed: MemoryMarshal.CreateFromPinnedArray creates a Memory<T> flagged as "already pinned", and Pin() then just computes the address. For your own MemoryManager<T> you define what Pin does.

cards/6/pairs/1/0: A native library keeps a buffer address between calls
cards/6/pairs/3/0: A buffer for the whole lifetime of the process

cards/7/title: The cost: holes in the heap
cards/7/body:
Compaction slides survivors to the start, freeing one contiguous area. A pinned object stands like a rock: it cannot be moved, and a gap is left in front of it. Many such gaps add up to fragmentation.

  • free memory exists, but in pieces: new objects and allocation chunks do not always fit;
  • the heap takes more than the live data;
  • worst of all are many small pins scattered across generation 0: that is the generation the collector most wants to compact cleanly.

A short pin during which no collection happened costs nothing. Long pins on fresh objects are what hurts.
cards/7/deep: The collector fights back: gaps in front of pinned objects become free blocks used for new chunks, and pinned objects from a young generation may stay in it (demotion) instead of being dragged into gen 2. But that is a workaround. You can see the problem in GC.GetGCMemoryInfo(): the PinnedObjectsCount and FragmentedBytes fields, and in a dump with the SOS command !gchandles.
cards/8/q: A server creates a byte[8192] per connection and keeps it pinned while the connection is open (minutes). What is wrong with that?
cards/8/options/0: Thousands of fresh pinned arrays riddle the young generations, and compaction cannot remove the holes
cards/8/options/1: Pinned arrays are not freed even after Free
cards/8/options/3: Nothing: 8 KB is a small object
cards/8/explain: The buffers are born in generation 0 among other objects and stay pinned for a long time. Each one has a gap around it that compaction cannot close. The cure is a pool of buffers allocated up front, ideally in the POH.
cards/8/wrong/2: Pinning itself is cheap: fixed is a mark on the stack, GCHandle is an entry in a table. Threads are suspended by a collection, not by a pin.
cards/9/title: The POH: a heap where nothing moves
cards/9/body:
Since .NET 5 the collector has a pinned object heap (POH). Objects in it never move, so they need no pinning and leave no holes in the SOH.

  • allocate an array with GC.AllocateArray<T>(length, pinned: true) or GC.AllocateUninitializedArray<T>(length, pinned: true) — without zeroing;
  • the POH is collected together with generation 2, that is, rarely;
  • allocating there is slower than usual: a free list instead of a pointer bump.

Takeaway: the POH is for long-lived buffers allocated once, such as a pool for sockets. Putting temporary arrays there is a bad idea.
cards/9/deep: Only arrays go to the POH. In .NET 5–7 the element type could not contain references (ArgumentException); .NET 8 lifted that restriction. Before the POH, pools of pinned buffers were made large (≥ 85,000 bytes) so they landed in the LOH, which is not compacted by default. Kestrel in ASP.NET Core keeps its memory blocks in the POH.
cards/10/q: Allocate the array straight in the pinned object heap
cards/10/explain: GC.AllocateArray with pinned: true puts the array in the POH. With pinned: false it is an ordinary array in the SOH or LOH — like new byte[n].
cards/11/q: What is true about the POH? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: The collector never moves objects in the POH
cards/11/options/1: The POH is collected together with generation 2
cards/11/options/2: Any object can go into the POH, not just arrays
cards/11/options/3: Allocating in the POH is cheaper than in generation 0
cards/11/options/4: The POH removes the SOH fragmentation that long pins would cause
cards/11/explain: The POH accepts only arrays via GC.AllocateArray and GC.AllocateUninitializedArray. Allocation there goes through a free list and costs more than a pointer bump, so the POH is for rare, long-lived buffers.
